Background Previous research has shown fluid replacement beverages ingested after exercise can affect hydration biomarkers. No specific hydration marker is universally accepted as an ideal rehydration parameter following strenuous exercise. Currently, changes in body mass are used as a parameter during post-exercise hydration. Additional parameters are needed to fully appreciate and better understand rehydration following strenuous exercise. This randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm trial assessed the effect of high-pH water on four biomarkers after exercise-induced dehydration. Methods One hundred healthy adults (50 M/50 F, 31 ± 6 years of age) were enrolled at a single clinical research center in Camden, NJ and completed this study with no adverse events. All individuals exercised in a warm environment (30 °C, 70% relative humidity) until their weight was reduced by a normally accepted level of 2.0 ± 0.2% due to perspiration, reflecting the effects of exercise in producing mild dehydration. Participants were randomized to rehydrate with an electrolyzed, high-pH (alkaline) water or standard water of equal volume (2% body weight) and assessed for an additional 2-h recovery period following exercise in order to assess any potential variations in measured parameters. The following biomarkers were assessed at baseline and during their recovery period: blood viscosity at high and low shear rates, plasma osmolality, bioimpedance, and body mass, as well as monitoring vital signs. Furthermore, a mixed model analysis was performed for additional validation. Results After exercise-induced dehydration, consumption of the electrolyzed, high-pH water reduced high-shear viscosity by an average of 6.30% compared to 3.36% with standard purified water ( p = 0.03). Other measured biomarkers (plasma osmolality, bioimpedance, and body mass change) revealed no significant difference between the two types of water for rehydration. However, a mixed model analysis validated the effect of high-pH water on high-shear viscosity when compared to standard purified water ( p = 0.0213) after controlling for covariates such as age and baseline values. Conclusions A significant difference in whole blood viscosity was detected in this study when assessing a high-pH, electrolyte water versus an acceptable standard purified water during the recovery phase following strenuous exercise-induced dehydration. Keywords Drinking water Rehydration solutions Fluid therapy Human physical conditioning Blood viscosity Essentia Water issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2016 Background Water is an essential nutrient for life, and hydration plays a critical role in human physical performance as well as in the prevention of chronic diseases. Dehydration is a well-accepted contributor to impaired human physical performance, resulting in guidelines established for fluid replacement in many professions involving significant physical activity, including athletes [ 1 ]. Performance impairments that are mediated by dehydration can produce untoward effects such as cardiovascular strain, heat strain, altered neurologic function and altered metabolic function [ 2 ]. Reductions in body mass by 2% or more due to perspiration during exercise have been well-established to be linked with impaired aerobic and physiologic performance. While this impairment involves metabolic, neurological, cardiovascular and important thermoregulatory factors, the primary limiting factor of exercise performance is cardiovascular drift, reflecting a shrinking cardiovascular reserve by reduced stroke volume and mean arterial pressure during intense or protracted exercise, coupled with an increase in heart rate [ 3 ]. Exercise-induced elevations in heart rate with a decrease in myocardial stroke volume can correlate closely with the degree of dehydration [ 2 ]. Dehydration has been shown to increase systemic vascular resistance by 17 ± 6% compared with euhydration during prolonged exercise ( p < 0.05) [ 4 ]. Numerous studies have evaluated beverage rehydration around exercise sessions, which have included supplementation with water, coconut water, juices, teas, sodas, as well as carbohydrate, electrolyte and glycerol beverages [ 5 – 9 ]. In a majority of these studies, fluid replacement beverages were administered orally after a dehydration challenge and the rehydration abilities of specific replacement beverages were assessed using biomarkers, physical performance evaluations and subjective questionnaires. One study involving 6 healthy males suggested that higher vs. lower concentrations of a carbohydrate-electrolyte solution were more effective in restoring hydration following exercise [ 5 ]. A study of 10 soccer players reported that exercise-induced changes in body mass and plasma volume were smaller with the ingestion of a carbohydrate-glycerol beverage than a carbohydrate beverage, highlighting improved hydration with the addition of glycerol [ 6 ]. Another study which monitored hydration biomarkers showed that coconut water did not hydrate significantly better than water alone [ 7 ]. Alkaline water (ALK) has been hypothesized to be superior to standard purified water in restoring rehydration and high-shear blood viscosity during a 2-h recovery period following exercise-induced dehydration; however, specific structured studies of one or multiple biomarkers during re-hydration following exercise have not established a gold standard biomarker for recovery period. Therefore, we designed a randomized, double-blind, parallel arm research study to characterize and compare the magnitude and rate of rehydration of high-pH electrolyzed water vs. standard purified water by assessing serial levels of a specific biomarker of whole blood viscosity at high-shear rate as a primary endpoint. In addition to measuring whole blood viscosity at high shear rate, the following secondary endpoints were assessed: low-shear blood viscosity, plasma osmolality, bioimpedance, and changes in body weight.

extracted_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm controlled study investigated the comparative rehydration efficacy of electrolyzed high-pH alkaline water (ALK) versus standard purified water (CON) on various hydration biomarkers in healthy adults following moderate exercise-induced dehydration. The primary finding was that ALK water significantly reduced high-shear whole blood viscosity and enhanced its restoration to pre-exercise baseline levels compared to CON water, while other markers like plasma osmolality, bioimpedance, and body mass showed no significant difference.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral rehydration therapy after exercise-induced dehydration, comparing electrolyzed high-pH alkaline water (ALK) with standard purified water (CON).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants exercised in a warm environment (30 °C, 70% relative humidity) until a 2.0 ± 0.2% body weight loss was achieved due to perspiration (mild dehydration). Rehydration involved consuming either electrolyzed high-pH alkaline water (ALK) or standard purified water (CON), with an equal volume equivalent to 2% of pre-exercise body weight (approximately 20 mL/kg), administered within 30 minutes. This was followed by a 120-minute (2-hour) recovery period. No dose-response comparisons or variations in rehydration volume/rate were reported beyond the two water types.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced by an average of 6.30% with high-pH alkaline water (ALK) compared to 3.36% with standard purified water (CON) after rehydration and recovery (p = 0.03). ALK significantly reduced and restored high-shear blood viscosity during a 120-min rehydration period by 87.50% more than CON. Mean systolic viscosity levels for ALK subjects returned to pre-exercise baseline by 60 minutes, while CON did not return by 120 minutes. Mixed model analysis validated this significant treatment effect (p = 0.02 or p = 0.0213).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates resistance to blood flow, critical for cardiovascular function, oxygen delivery, and reflects intravascular hydration status, influenced by hematocrit levels and red cell deformability.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post exercise-induced dehydration during a 2-hour recovery period following rehydration with high-pH alkaline water compared to standard purified water.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Improved cardiovascular function and reduced cardiovascular strain; associated with better rehydration status, enhanced rehydration efficiency, and potentially improved physical performance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Although the average percentage change was 9.35% for ALK vs. 5.43% for CON, and a trend for faster decrease with ALK was observed, no significant difference or treatment effect was found between electrolyzed high-pH water and standard purified water in mixed model analyses.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates resistance to blood flow, particularly at slower flow rates, impacting microcirculation and blood fluidity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post exercise-induced dehydration during a 2-hour recovery period following rehydration with high-pH alkaline water compared to standard purified water.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a distinguishing indicator of rehydration efficacy between high-pH and standard water in this context, despite a numerical trend towards greater reduction with ALK.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference was observed between electrolyzed high-pH water (ALK) and standard purified water (CON) in any analyses performed in this study, including mixed model analyses comparing the percent change during rehydration.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the concentration of osmotically active particles/solutes in plasma, serving as a key indicator of hydration status and electrolyte balance, regulating body fluid balance.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post exercise-induced dehydration during a 2-hour recovery period following rehydration with high-pH alkaline water compared to standard purified water.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a primary or differentially sensitive indicator of improved rehydration efficacy between high-pH and standard water in this specific comparison, nor considered a consistent 'gold standard' for all hydration assessment requirements.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Bioelectrical Impedance (indices including impedance, reactance, capacitance, phase angle, total body water, intracellular water, and extracellular water)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference or treatment effect was found between electrolyzed high-pH water (ALK) and standard purified water (CON) on any bioimpedance indices in mixed model analyses, despite impedance showing a trend for a faster increase (greater positive slope) for ALK compared to CON.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the body's resistance to electrical current, used to estimate body composition and hydration levels, including total body water and its distribution across fluid compartments.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post exercise-induced dehydration during a 2-hour recovery period following rehydration with high-pH alkaline water compared to standard purified water.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a primary or significantly differentiating indicator of improved rehydration efficacy in this specific comparison; may not accurately predict changes in body water with acute, small changes (e.g., 2% body mass).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: While 2.0 ± 0.2% body weight was lost during exercise-induced dehydration and 2% body weight was replaced during rehydration, no significant difference in body mass change was observed between electrolyzed high-pH water and standard purified water during the recovery period.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Directly reflects the net fluid balance of the body, indicating the degree of dehydration or rehydration, and total body water losses and gains.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post exercise-induced dehydration during a 2-hour recovery period following rehydration with high-pH alkaline water compared to standard purified water.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A primary and accurate indicator for quantifying dehydration level and monitoring rehydration effectiveness; however, in this study, it did not differentiate between the two rehydration methods.
